hook.text: Even if emissions stopped today, decades of warming are already locked in.

buildup.text: Cities build sea walls, plant shade trees, and redesign drainage for bigger storms.

discovery.text: Farmers switch to drought-resistant crops. Architects design buildings for extreme heat.

twist.text: Rich nations can afford to adapt. Poor nations — who emit the least — often cannot.

climax.text: Adaptation buys time. It doesn't fix the root cause.

punchline.text: We can't stop the wave, but we can build higher.

quiz.question: Why is adaptation necessary even if emissions drop?
options: Past emissions have already locked in warming

details.summary: Climate adaptation involves adjusting infrastructure, agriculture, and social systems to cope with warming that is already unavoidable. Examples include sea walls, drought-resistant crops, upgraded storm drainage, and heat action plans for cities.
details.whyItMatters: Even if emissions stopped today, past warming commits the world to decades of further change. Adaptation is no longer optional — it is urgent survival planning.
takeaways: Some warming is already locked in regardless of future emissions
Adaptation and mitigation must happen simultaneously
Developing countries need most adaptation but have the least funding

faq.question: How much does climate adaptation cost?
faq.answer: The UN estimates developing countries alone need 160 to 340 billion dollars per year for adaptation by 2030. Current international adaptation finance is roughly 20 billion per year, creating a massive and growing gap.

faq.question: What is the difference between adaptation and mitigation?
faq.answer: Mitigation reduces greenhouse gas emissions to slow warming. Adaptation prepares for the warming that is already happening or unavoidable. Both are essential: mitigation prevents the worst outcomes, and adaptation manages the impacts we cannot avoid.
